stem: A 46-year-old man is evaluated for intermittent chest pain and progressive dyspnea.  Noninvasive cardiac testing is nondiagnostic, and a heart catheterization is performed.  During the procedure, the catheter tip is positioned in various cardiac chambers and the great vessels to measure pressure changes.  At a specific location, the catheter tip records a maximum pressure of 25 mm Hg and minimum of 2 mm Hg during each cardiac cycle.  When the catheter is advanced further, the pressure readings change to a maximum of 25 mm Hg and a minimum of 10 mm Hg.  Assuming the results of the procedure are normal, the first set of readings were most likely obtained from which of the following locations?​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​
explanation:
Cardiac catheterization can be used to measure intracardiac pressures and evaluate cardiac disease.  During right-sided heart catheterization, a catheter is inserted into the systemic venous circulation and guided toward the heart.  Once in the heart, the location of the catheter tip can be determined by the pressure readings as follows:

  1. The pressure in the right atrium is representative of central venous pressure and normally ranges from 2-8 mm Hg (Choice D).

  2. As the catheter advances across the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, a pulsatile waveform appears.  The peak (systolic) pressure occurs during right ventricular contraction and is approximately 25 mm Hg under normal conditions.  The lowest (diastolic) pressure is slightly lower than the right atrial pressure to allow diastolic filling from the right atrium.  Therefore, right ventricular pressure typically cycles between approximately 2 and 25 mm Hg.

  3. As the catheter advances across the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary artery, the pressure waveform shows a sudden increase in diastolic pressure to approximately 10 mm Hg with no change in systolic pressure (Choice C).  This rise in diastolic pressure is caused by the closed pulmonic valve trapping blood in the pulmonary vasculature against pulmonary vascular resistance.

  4. When the catheter is advanced further and lodged into a branch of the pulmonary artery, the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is measured.  The PCWP is a close approximation of left atrial pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and typically ranges from 6-12 mm Hg (Choice A).

(Choice B)  Left ventricular pressures are much higher than right ventricular pressures because systemic vascular resistance is much higher than pulmonary vascular resistance.  The normal left ventricular systolic pressure is approximately 120 mm Hg (and diastolic pressure ranges from 6-12 mm Hg, as reflected by PCWP).

Educational objective:Right ventricular pressure cycles between approximately 2 mm Hg (during diastole) and 25 mm Hg (during systole).  Left ventricular pressures are much higher than right ventricular pressures because systemic vascular resistance is much higher than pulmonary vascular resistance.​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​
